title: Kitchen Fitting Cost Per Unit UK: What to Budget
description: Kitchen fitting cost per unit UK explained: typical installation prices, what’s included, and how layout, materials, plumbing and electrics affect your quote.
targetKeyword: kitchen fitting cost per unit uk

blocks.text: Searching for the kitchen fitting cost per unit in the UK can give you a useful starting point, but it is not a complete quote. Kitchen installers may price by cabinet, by day, by room size or as one fixed project price. As a rough guide, standard kitchen cabinet installation labour may typically be around £150 to £300 per unit, while larger, rigid, tall or more complicated units may be around £250 to £500 or more. Every project differs, and these figures may exclude cabinets, worktops, appliances and additional trades; request a free, no-obligation quote from BMB Renovation for accurate pricing in its service areas.
What does a kitchen fitting cost per unit include?

A per-unit installation price may cover assembling or positioning the cabinet, securing it to the wall or floor, levelling it and fitting doors, drawer fronts and basic hardware. For a base unit, it may also include preparing the cabinet for a sink or appliance, although the exact scope should be confirmed before work starts. Wall units can require additional care where walls are uneven or fixings need strengthening. Tall larder, housing and integrated-appliance units can take longer because they need accurate alignment with neighbouring cabinets and surrounding finishes.

items: Standard base or wall cabinet installation: as a rough guide, typically around £150–£300 per unit for labour.
Tall, larder or integrated appliance housing: as a rough guide, typically around £250–£500 or more per unit.
Flat-pack furniture can require additional assembly time, particularly if parts are missing, damaged or difficult to align.
Rigid or pre-assembled units may reduce assembly time on site, although installation requirements still vary.

These are broad UK guide prices, not fixed rates. Every project differs, and access, location, VAT and the agreed scope can change the final figure; request a free, no-obligation quote for accurate pricing.

Why the number of units is not the whole story

Multiplying a unit rate by the number of cupboards can make a quote appear straightforward, but kitchens contain several tasks that do not fit neatly into a per-unit calculation. Removing the old kitchen, protecting floors, assembling furniture, scribing panels, fitting plinths and installing end panels all take time. A small kitchen with difficult access can cost more to fit than a larger, open room. Similarly, a simple run of base cabinets may take less time than a U-shaped layout with multiple corners, a peninsula, tall housings and several integrated appliances.
Layout and access factors that affect labour

The layout can have a significant effect on the final installation price. Corners need careful measuring and may require corner mechanisms or filler panels. Islands and peninsulas can involve extra units, decorative panels and service routes. Uneven floors and walls can mean more scribing and adjustment, particularly in older homes. Access also matters: stairs, restricted parking, long carrying distances and limited working space can add time without adding units. Ask whether the quotation includes delivery handling, rubbish removal, protection of existing areas and final adjustment of doors and drawers.
How materials and cabinet type change the price

The furniture itself can vary considerably in price, so it is important to separate the cost of the units from fitting labour. Basic melamine-faced cabinets and standard laminate doors may be more economical than painted timber, solid wood, framed, handleless or bespoke furniture. Delicate finishes may require slower installation and more care to avoid marking. Worktops create another distinction: laminate worktops can often be cut and fitted by the kitchen installer, while quartz, granite and some porcelain surfaces may need specialist templating and installation. Curved worktops, upstands, splashbacks and unusual cut-outs should be listed separately in the quote.

items: Cabinets and doors: check whether these are priced separately from fitting.
Worktops: laminate, timber, compact laminate and stone can have different fitting requirements.
Handles and hinges: confirm whether fitting is included, as upgraded mechanisms or push-to-open systems can add labour.
Integrated appliances: allow for housing, ventilation, panels and connections individually.
Splashbacks and tiling: these are often measured by area rather than by cabinet unit and may need a separate allowance.

blocks.text: Additional trades that can change the final kitchen quote

A kitchen replacement can involve more than cabinet installation. Moving a sink, dishwasher or washing machine may require plumbing and alterations to waste pipes. Changing the cooker position may involve electrical work, gas work by a suitably qualified professional where applicable, or changes to ventilation. New sockets, lighting, an extractor, flooring, plastering, decorating and tiling can all sit outside a basic per-unit fitting rate. If walls need repairing after the old cabinets are removed, that preparation should be priced before fitting begins. A clear quotation should show what is included, excluded and provisional.

When comparing quotes, provide each installer with the same cabinet plan, unit count, appliance list and worktop specification. Ask for separate lines for removal, installation, plumbing, electrical work, tiling, flooring, decorating, delivery and waste disposal. Check whether prices include VAT and whether the installer is supplying materials or fitting items you have bought yourself. It is also sensible to ask who is responsible for measuring, checking appliance requirements and resolving damaged or missing parts. faq.q: What is the average kitchen fitting cost per unit in the UK?
faq.a: As a rough guide, standard cabinet installation labour may typically be around £150–£300 per unit. Tall, integrated or complex units may be around £250–£500 or more. Every project differs, and these figures commonly exclude kitchen furniture and additional trades; request a free, no-obligation quote from BMB Renovation for accurate pricing in its service areas.

faq.q: Is kitchen fitting charged per unit or by the day?
faq.a: Both approaches may be used. Per-unit pricing can suit a straightforward installation, while a daily rate or fixed project price may be more suitable where there is removal, plumbing, tiling, electrical work or extensive preparation.

faq.q: Does the cost per kitchen unit include appliances?
faq.a: Often it does not. Appliance supply may be separate, and installation may also be separate if connections, housing alterations, ventilation or electrical work are required. Check each appliance and connection on the written quote.

faq.q: What makes kitchen fitting more expensive?
faq.a: Complex layouts, uneven walls or floors, islands, tall units, bespoke finishes, stone worktops, appliance changes, plumbing, electrics, tiling, flooring and plastering can all increase the total cost.

faq.q: How can I get an accurate kitchen fitting price?
faq.a: Provide a measured plan, cabinet schedule, appliance list and worktop details, then ask for a written quote that separates fitting, removal, materials and additional trades. A site visit can help check access and the condition of the room. BMB Renovation offers free, no-obligation quotes.
